title: Building in public before the business is obvious
dek: Notes on SIndustries as a company-of-one exploration: systems first, proof of movement, and public signal before the model fully resolves.
body:
The temptation when starting a company is to wait until things are ready. Get the model right. Get the product right. Then go public. The problem with that approach is you never get feedback until it's expensive to change anything.

SIndustries is an experiment in the opposite direction. Build in public before the business is obvious. Put the systems out there while the model is still forming. Let the signal from the outside world shape what it becomes, not confirm a thesis I already decided on.

The framing is important. I'm not building in public to perform. I'm doing it to learn faster. There's a difference. Performance is about curating a narrative. Learning is about running experiments and publishing results whether they're flattering or not.

Right now the model is: systems that compound, explorations that test reality, and signals that prove momentum. That's deliberately broad because I don't have enough evidence yet to narrow it. The explorations are designed to generate that evidence.

Drop 1 will tell me whether I can run a product cycle end to end. Social content will tell me what topics earn attention. Product market scans will tell me where there are real gaps worth pursuing. Each one is a bet on a question, not a commitment to an answer.

The NZ personal banking app is the clearest version of this so far. It started as a concept about household budgeting and open banking constraints, then became a working mobile build connected to live bank data. Accounts, cards, balance alerts, spending breakdowns, recategorisation, and transaction detail surfaces now exist in the product instead of the plan. That changes the kind of learning available: the question moves from whether the idea is plausible to whether the live-data flow actually helps a household make better decisions.

The thing I keep coming back to: most people building companies are building in secret, which means they're building with incomplete information. Building in public is a structural advantage if you use the signal rather than just chase the audience.

I'll know this approach is working when the public signals start producing unexpected inputs — people pointing at things I hadn't considered, connections I wouldn't have made, doors that open because someone saw what I was doing and wanted to be part of it. That's the outcome I'm optimising for.
